chapter 01 · transformer — part 3 of 5

Position

Attention cannot see order, so order has to be added. Then: the same layer pointed at images, graphs and contact matrices, and how it compares with the architectures it replaced.

Position: the one thing attention cannot see

Look back at the formula and try to find the index i in it. It isn't there. Scores depend on q and k, the output is a sum over all positions — nothing anywhere refers to where a token sits. Shuffle the inputs and the outputs come back shuffled the same way, otherwise unchanged. Attention is permutation-equivariant, which means "dog bites man" and "man bites dog" are, to a bare attention layer, the same input. Position has to be injected by hand:

Why not just append the position as a number? It is the first thing anyone tries, and it fails three ways: the value is unbounded (position 4000 arrives as a feature 4000× larger than position 1 and swamps the layer norm), it is one dimension against thousands of content dimensions, and it does not generalise — a model trained to 2 048 has never seen the number 5 000 and has no reason to treat it sensibly. You want something bounded, high-dimensional, and smooth in position. Sinusoids are all three.

Measure it. practice p2 trains two identical Vision Transformers on MNIST, one with the positional encoding switched off, then shuffles the image patches at test time. With position: 95.51 % → 84.57 %. Without: 92.28 % → 92.28 %, a delta of exactly +0.00 — the layer cannot see the shuffle because it only ever received a set.

Said plainly: it is a map out of ℕ

Strip the sinusoids away and absolute positional encoding is one move, with a type signature worth writing down:

PE : ℕ ⟶ ℝ^d_model      # one dimension in, thousands out

Which is the same trade as part 0, applied to position instead of to data: spend dimensions, buy a space where the thing you want is easy to express. A single integer has no room for "three tokens back" to be a direction; d_model of them do.

That also sharpens the earlier objection. Appending the raw index is not a different idea — it is this map with d = 1, which is why all three of its failures are symptoms of the same thing: the codomain was too small.

Why add it, and not multiply

Having built bi the right width, there are two obvious ways to put it in:

Addition is the only one of the two that survives the projection. Because Wq is linear, Wq(a + e) = Wqa + Wqe — content and position pass through as separate summands, and the score expands into four terms, one of them a pure position–position term carrying the offset. That is what the next subsection's rotation argument needs in order to reach the score at all.

A product does not split: Wq(a ⊙ p) cannot be separated into a content part and a position part. Worse, ⊙ gates — a small entry in Pw suppresses that feature at that position no matter which token is sitting there. Position would be scaling meaning rather than offsetting it.

Why sinusoids, and not any other bounded code

"Continuous binary counter" explains why the pattern never repeats, but not why these functions. The real reason is one property, and it is the whole design:

PE(pos)2i   = sin(ωi · pos)        ωi = 1 / 100002i/d
PE(pos)2i+1 = cos(ωi · pos)

# take any fixed offset k. For each (sin, cos) pair:

[ sin(ω(pos+k)) ]   [ cos ωk   sin ωk ] [ sin(ω·pos) ]
[ cos(ω(pos+k)) ] = [ -sin ωk  cos ωk ] [ cos(ω·pos) ]
                     └──── R(ωk) ────┘   # a rotation. Depends on k, NOT on pos.

PE(pos+k) is a fixed linear function of PE(pos). Each (sin, cos) pair is a 2D vector spinning at its own rate, and moving k steps rotates every pair by an angle that depends only on k. So a single learned linear map — which is exactly what Wq and Wk are — can implement "attend three tokens back", and the same map works at position 5 and position 500.

Which makes RoPE a small step, not a new idea. Sinusoidal encoding gives you rotation-by-position, then adds it to the input and hopes the projections recover it. RoPE applies the same rotation directly to q and k. Then in the score the two rotations meet:

(Rmq) · (Rnk)  =  q ᵀRmᵀRn k  =  q ᵀRn−m k      # absolute positions cancel

The score depends only on n − m, the relative offset. Nothing is added to the residual stream, nothing has to be recovered, and a distance of 3 means the same thing at position 10 and position 10 000 — which is why it extrapolates past the training length so much better.

Two things about that slide have dated, and both are worth knowing. "Hand-crafted" is no longer the norm — GPT-2 and BERT learned absolute position embeddings instead, and current models overwhelmingly use RoPE, which doesn't add anything to ai at all. RoPE rotates q and k by an angle proportional to position, so the dot product between them ends up depending only on their relative distance — which is usually what actually matters, and extrapolates to lengths never seen in training far better than absolute encodings do.

And the choice to add rather than concatenate looks lossy at first — you're summing position into the same coordinates that carry meaning. It works because d_model is large: in a few thousand dimensions there is ample room for position and content to occupy near-orthogonal subspaces, and the projections can read either one back out. Concatenating would have cost extra width for the same effect.

Those sinusoids are a Fourier basis

Set the two definitions next to each other and the resemblance is not a coincidence:

So the d_model coordinates of PE(pos) are not an arbitrary bounded code — they are a frequency decomposition of the position index, one (sin, cos) pair per frequency. The exponent 2i/D sweeps those frequencies geometrically, and that is what sets the usable range:

Every term written out, and the frequency ladder it spans

Which lets you read the matrix two ways, and both are useful:

Two properties fall out of that reading, and they are the design.

  • 频域中，P 的维度互相之间正交. Different frequency channels are mutually orthogonal, so each carries information the others cannot — nothing is wasted on duplication, and the projections can pick out one scale without disturbing another.
  • 在更大的范围内有更小的“原子”频率. The geometric sweep puts very low frequencies in the code, and a low frequency is a long period. Longer period, more positions addressable before the pattern wraps — which is precisely the knob you turn to extend context length.
And this is where “distance” turns into “angle”

What the score actually does with P

Earlier this page claimed that adding position makes the score split into four terms. Here is that expansion, and it is where the modern position schemes come from:

termwhat it asks
XqWWᵀXkᵀcontent–content — the only term that would exist without position. "Is this the token I want?"
XqWWᵀPkᵀcontent–position — "given what I am, which slot should I look at?"
PqWWᵀXkᵀposition–content — "given where I am, which token should I look for?"
PqWWᵀPkᵀposition–position — pure geometry, and the only one that can encode "three tokens back"

The bottom of that figure works on the fourth term. If f(q,k) can be made to depend on q−k alone, the score stops caring about absolute location. Force that, replace the leftover absolute pieces with learned vectors u and v, and you get Transformer-XL's relative encoding — the final line of the figure.

RoPE takes the other route from the same expansion. Instead of adding P and then repairing the four terms, it declines to add anything and rotates q and k themselves, so only q−k can ever survive. In the lecture's complex notation that is one line:

Which explains the hedge two subsections ago. Sinusoidal encoding hopes the projections recover position from a sum of four entangled terms; RoPE removes the hope by making three of them impossible to write down.

The same layer, other modalities

Nothing in the derivation assumed language. Attention needs only a set of vectors — so anything you can express that way is fair game:

That reframing was enough to rebuild much of computer vision around attention:

Spot the disguise in the SAGAN diagram. Those three 1×1 convolutions producing f(x), g(x), h(x) are Wq, Wk, Wv — a 1×1 convolution is precisely a per-position linear projection, applied identically at every location. Follow the arrows: f and g multiply and softmax into an attention map, which then weights h. It is the equation you already know, drawn in the vocabulary of convnets.

Speech fits the same mould, but it's where the O(n²) bill comes due:

That slide is more current than it looks. Truncated attention is the ancestor of every long-context method in production today — sliding-window attention, Longformer's local-plus-global pattern, and the sparse and linear attention families all make the same bet, that most of the L × L matrix isn't worth computing. (FlashAttention is the exception that proves the rule: it keeps every entry and instead avoids ever writing the matrix to memory.) This is the same O(n²) wall flagged back at the attention matrix, and in §3 it reappears as the constraint that governs how much an agent can hold in context.

Self-attention vs CNN: the same operation, one with its receptive field frozen

Once an image is a vector set, the obvious question is what separates attention from the convolution that ruled vision for a decade. The answer is sharper than "they're different architectures":

That isn't just an analogy — it holds formally:

That slide asserts it. The construction behind it is worth seeing, because it is short. Start by throwing away everything a head knows about content — keep only the relative-position term from the four-term expansion:

Now choose the relative encoding and that vector to complete a square:

So one head can be pinned to one offset. Read the attention matrix underneath: with Δ = −2 the mass sits on a single diagonal band, two positions back, at every query. That is a shift. In two dimensions Rδ⃗ = (‖δ⃗‖², δ₁, δ₂) gives the same result for a pixel offset Δ⃗(h) — one head, one tap of a kernel.

That is what "strict subset" means, precisely. Not "attention is a bit like convolution" — a multi-head self-attention layer with relative position encoding and Nh heads can represent any convolutional layer whose kernel has Nh taps. The heads supply the kernel positions, the value projections supply the weights. And note which ingredient carries it: relative position encoding. The construction needs q − k; absolute encodings cannot state "two back" as one fact.

Being the more flexible model is not automatically an advantage, and the data settles it:

Reproduce the shape of it on a laptop. practice p2 runs a small CNN and a ViT at the same budget over a growing slice of MNIST. The gap closes monotonically — −19.4 points at N = 1 000, −2.9 at N = 60 000 — without ever crossing, because all of MNIST sits inside the small-data regime. The slope is the argument; the crossover needs the 100 M images this chart has.

This chart is the whole architecture story of the last decade, in one picture. A CNN's hard-coded locality is a prior — free knowledge, handed over before training starts, that nearby pixels belong together. When data is scarce that prior is worth more than anything the model could induce, so the CNN wins. When data is abundant the same prior becomes a ceiling: the model is forbidden from learning a better rule than the one you imposed. Attention has less built in and therefore needs more data — and given that data, it learns a rule your kernel size could never encode.

The identical trade played out in language: LSTMs carried a strong sequential prior and beat early transformers on small corpora, then lost decisively once corpora reached internet scale. It's the reason §2's story is about scale rather than about cleverer architectures — the flexible model plus more data beats the constrained model, as soon as you can afford the data.

Self-attention vs RNN: why the recurrence went away

Before attention, sequences meant recurrence: carry a memory vector forward, one step at a time. The slide puts the two side by side, and the two red annotations are the entire argument:

Notice that attention is not the cheaper option. An RNN layer costs O(n) with a fixed-size state; attention costs O(n²) and stores the whole matrix. What attention did was convert a latency problem into a throughput problem — and throughput is something you can buy more GPUs for, while a sequential dependency is something no amount of hardware can remove. That trade is the entire reason the architecture won.

The paper cited on that slide closes the loop. "Transformers are RNNs" (arXiv:2006.16236) shows that with linear attention, an autoregressive transformer is expressible as an RNN with constant-size state. And this isn't only a theoretical curiosity — recall from earlier that generation is sequential anyway: a decoding transformer with a KV cache is already a recurrent model whose state happens to grow. The RNN never really lost at inference. It lost at training, which is where the parallelism was worth having.

Graphs: attention with the edges supplied

One last case, and it retro-fits everything above into a single idea. A graph is already a set of vectors — one per node — so attention applies directly. But a graph also tells you something extra: which pairs are actually related.

The unifying idea: structure enters through the mask. Every variant in this whole section is the same layer with a different rule about which cells of the score matrix are allowed to be non-zero.

  • No mask → every position sees every other. Plain self-attention, an encoder, BERT.
  • Causal mask → position i sees only ≤ i. Language modelling, every decoder, step 4 below.
  • Window mask → each position sees a local range. Truncated attention for speech, and every sliding-window long-context scheme.
  • Adjacency mask → only connected nodes. Graph attention networks.
  • Fixed offset per head → the convolution, as the Cordonnier construction showed.

So the honest one-line summary of the last several subsections: attention is a general mechanism for routing information between positions, and each architecture is a prior about which routes are worth allowing. Choose the mask and you've chosen the architecture.

Worked case: a Hi-C contact matrix

The course's capstone is a 3D-genomics agent, so it is worth doing one domain case properly. Say the input is an n × n Hi-C contact matrix. Attention needs a set of vectors — so the only question that matters is: what is one token? There are three defensible answers, and they build different models.

designone token is…the contact matrix is…good for
patches
ViT-style		a tile of the map, e.g. 16×16 bins, flattenedthe input imagelearning map structure itself — denoising, resolution enhancement, calling loops and TADs. The shape Hi-C foundation models take
bins
graph-style		one genomic bin, carrying its own features (epigenomic tracks, say)an attention bias or mask over bin pairs — exactly “let the edges decide the matrix” abovereasoning over loci when you already trust the contacts and want to propagate signal along them
sequence
Akita / Orca-style		a bin of DNA sequencethe target, not the input — you predict itasking what the sequence itself determines about folding

Will it be embedded? Yes — always, and that is not optional. Attention consumes vectors of width d_model, so whatever you choose as a token, something has to produce that vector. The only difference from text is how:

inputembedding is…
texta lookup table: a discrete vocabulary indexes a learned row
a Hi-C patch, or any continuous inputa linear projection: flatten the 16×16 tile to 256 numbers, multiply by a learned 256 × d_model matrix

Both are "the embedding layer" and both are learned. A vocabulary lookup is just a matmul with a one-hot vector, so mechanically they are the same operation — Hi-C simply skips the one-hot. And position still has to be injected: for patches it is 2D (which row-block, which column-block), not the 1D offset text uses.

But they do different jobs — four differences worth knowing
English wordsHi-C patches
inputdiscrete — a finite vocabulary (~50k). Each token owns a separate learned row; nothing lies between cat and dogcontinuous — no vocabulary at all. Two similar tiles get similar vectors automatically, because a linear map is smooth, and a tile never seen still embeds sensibly
size50 000 × 4096 ≈ 200M parameters — often the single largest matrix in a small model256 × 4096 ≈ 1M — negligible
what it learnsmeaning. It is a knowledge store; the famous king − man + woman ≈ queen geometry lives in this tablefeatures. It is a feature extractor, much closer to the first convolution layer of a CNN than to a dictionary
tied to the output?often yes — the same matrix runs in reverse to produce logits over the same vocabularyonly if you are reconstructing patches, which masked-patch models do. Otherwise there is no vocabulary to predict back into

One practical consequence of the discrete/continuous split: continuous inputs must be scaled before projection and discrete ones need not be. A lookup row is whatever training made it; a raw Hi-C tile spans orders of magnitude and will dominate or vanish depending on where on the diagonal it came from. That is the same normalization point as trap 2 below, arriving one step earlier in the pipeline.

Three things that will bite you, in this order

  1. n² is not survivable at genomic scale. At 10 kb bins the human genome is ~300 000 bins — 9 × 10¹⁰ pairs for one score matrix. This is the same wall ViT hit at 224×224 pixels, and the same answer applies: patches, windows, or sparse attention are mandatory, not an optimisation. Decide your receptive field before anything else; it fixes what questions the model can even pose.
  2. The diagonal dominates — for real this time. Contact frequency decays as a power law with genomic distance, so raw counts near the diagonal swamp everything. Feed those in and the model learns distance and nothing else. Normalize first — observed/expected, or distance-stratified — and note the irony: this is the same failure as the raw dot product above, where aⁱ·aⁱ necessarily dominated its row. Different cause, identical symptom.
  3. Hi-C is symmetric; attention is not. contact(i,j) = contact(j,i), but Wᑫ ≠ Wᵏ exists precisely so that αi,j ≠ αj,i. That is not a conflict — it means a bin-level model can learn directional relations the matrix itself cannot express. Worth knowing you have that freedom, and worth checking whether your evaluation assumes symmetry when your model no longer has it.

Which design is right depends on the question, and that decision belongs to the capstone rather than this page. The point here is narrower: nothing about attention changed. Vectors in, vectors out, scores from queries and keys. Only the answer to “what is one token?” moved.

Go and run one. Attention is the rare idea where the interactive explanations are genuinely better than the prose — including this page's. Seven, ordered by how much work they ask of you. The first two are hands-on labs in this repo; the third is the source of this page's own figures. All verified live 2026-10-09.

p0 · attention by hand
in this repo · open the notebook in Colab		 See it, then build it. A notebook steps through one attention layer with numbers small enough to check by hand — change a value, re-run, watch the pattern move. Then attention_lab.py makes you implement single-head, multi-head and masked attention yourself, checked against your own longhand loop. The mechanism, in your hands. Written for exactly this point — you have watched the lectures and want to do it. It makes you prove the two things slides cannot: that heads never mix (perturb one head's keys, the others must come out bit-identical) and that masking makes the past independent of the future (rewrite later tokens, earlier outputs must not move). It also measures why 1/√d_k exists instead of asserting it.

What multi-head is FOR. p0 proves heads cannot mix; this shows why that matters — the model splits one algorithm across two layers, a previous-token head in layer 0 feeding induction heads in layer 1, and neither half works alone. It also carries the lesson that cost me a wrong result: the first version scored every head at 0.9 because a fixed-period task lets a positional reflex masquerade as content matching. The control column is the exercise.

If attention still feels like notation after the first two, do the puzzles rather than re-reading. The gap is usually not "what are Q, K, V" but "what class of computation does this buy" — and that one is only closed by writing something in it.
